claim: IMPDH mediates the first committed step in guanine nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) mediates the first committed step in guanine nucleotide biosynthesis and plays important roles in cellular proliferation and the immune response.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about IMPDH function.

claim: IMPDH plays important roles in cellular proliferation and the immune response.
source: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) mediates the first committed step in guanine nucleotide biosynthesis and plays important roles in cellular proliferation and the immune response.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is cited in the introduction.

claim: IMPDH reversibly polymerizes in cells and tissues in response to changes in metabolic demand.
source: IMPDH reversibly polymerizes in cells and tissues in response to changes in metabolic demand.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Self-assembly of metabolic enzymes is a general mechanism for regulating activity.
source: Self-assembly of metabolic enzymes is increasingly recognized as a general mechanism for regulating activity, typically by stabilizing specific conformations of an enzyme, but the regulatory role of IMPDH filaments has remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies on metabolic enzyme assembly.

claim: The regulatory role of IMPDH filaments has remained unclear.
source: Self-assembly of metabolic enzymes is increasingly recognized as a general mechanism for regulating activity, typically by stabilizing specific conformations of an enzyme, but the regulatory role of IMPDH filaments has remained unclear.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The structures define the mechanism of filament assembly.
source: The structures define the mechanism of filament assembly, and reveal how filament-dependent allosteric regulation of IMPDH2 makes the enzyme less sensitive to feedback inhibition, explaining why assembly occurs under physiological conditions that require expansion of guanine nucleotide pools.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Filament-dependent allosteric regulation of IMPDH2 makes the enzyme less sensitive to feedback inhibition.
source: The structures define the mechanism of filament assembly, and reveal how filament-dependent allosteric regulation of IMPDH2 makes the enzyme less sensitive to feedback inhibition, explaining why assembly occurs under physiological conditions that require expansion of guanine nucleotide pools.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural and biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: IMPDH assembly occurs under physiological conditions that require expansion of guanine nucleotide pools.
source: The structures define the mechanism of filament assembly, and reveal how filament-dependent allosteric regulation of IMPDH2 makes the enzyme less sensitive to feedback inhibition, explaining why assembly occurs under physiological conditions that require expansion of guanine nucleotide pools.
evidence: This is supported by the structural and biochemical findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tuning sensitivity to an allosteric inhibitor distinguishes IMPDH from other metabolic filaments.
source: Tuning sensitivity to an allosteric inhibitor distinguishes IMPDH from other metabolic filaments, and highlights the diversity of regulatory outcomes that can emerge from self-assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing IMPDH regulation to other known metabolic filaments.

claim: Under most conditions, cells rely on salvage pathways to regenerate degradation products and maintain nucleotide pools.
source: Under most conditions, cells rely on salvage pathways to regenerate degradation products and maintain nucleotide pools.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleotide metabolism.

claim: When nucleotide demand is high, flux through de novo nucleotide biosynthesis pathways is up-regulated.
source: However when nucleotide demand is high, for example during cellular proliferation, flux through de novo nucleotide biosynthesis pathways is up-regulated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleotide metabolism supported by the citation (Lane and Fan, 2015).

claim: IMPDH catalyzes the first committed step in guanine nucleotide synthesis.
source: The enzyme IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH) catalyzes the first committed step in guanine nucleotide synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IMPDH function.

claim: Balancing the flux through parallel adenine and guanine synthesis pathways is essential for cellular homeostasis.
source: Balancing the flux through these parallel synthesis pathways, which share the precursor inosine monophosphate (IMP), is essential for cellular homeostasis (Figure 1A) (Allison and Eugui, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Allison and Eugui, 2000) and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: IMPDH is regulated transcriptionally, post-translationally, and allosterically.
source: IMPDH is regulated transcriptionally, post-translationally, and allosterically (Hedstrom, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Hedstrom, 2009).

claim: In vertebrates, two IMPDH isoforms (83% identical in humans) have differential expression patterns.
source: In vertebrates, two IMPDH isoforms, (83% identical in humans), have differential expression patterns (Collart and Huberman, 1988; Natsumeda et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Collart and Huberman, 1988; Natsumeda et al., 1990).

claim: IMPDH1 is constitutively expressed at low levels in most tissues.
source: IMPDH1 is constitutively expressed at low levels in most tissues, while IMPDH2 is generally upregulated in proliferating tissues (Carr et al., 1993; Hager et al., 1995; Jackson et al., 1975; Senda and Natsumeda, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Carr et al., 1993; Hager et al., 1995; Jackson et al., 1975; Senda and Natsumeda, 1994).

claim: IMPDH2 is generally upregulated in proliferating tissues.
source: IMPDH1 is constitutively expressed at low levels in most tissues, while IMPDH2 is generally upregulated in proliferating tissues (Carr et al., 1993; Hager et al., 1995; Jackson et al., 1975; Senda and Natsumeda, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Carr et al., 1993; Hager et al., 1995; Jackson et al., 1975; Senda and Natsumeda, 1994).

claim: In mice, knockout of IMPDH1 results in only very minor vision defects.
source: In mice, knockout of IMPDH1 results in only very minor vision defects, whereas knockout of IMPDH2 is embryonic lethal (Aherne et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2003; Gu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Aherne et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2003; Gu et al., 2000).

claim: Knockout of IMPDH2 is embryonic lethal in mice.
source: In mice, knockout of IMPDH1 results in only very minor vision defects, whereas knockout of IMPDH2 is embryonic lethal (Aherne et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2003; Gu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Aherne et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2003; Gu et al., 2000).

claim: IMPDH reversibly assembles into filaments in vertebrate cells and tissues.
source: IMPDH reversibly assembles into filaments in vertebrate cells and tissues, which is thought to provide an additional layer of regulation (Carcamo et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2006; Thomas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Carcamo et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2006; Thomas et al., 2012).

claim: Self-assembly into filamentous polymers has been observed in cells for a large number of metabolic enzymes.
source: Self-assembly into filamentous polymers has recently been observed in cells for a large number of metabolic enzymes (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009; Noree et al., 2019; Noree et al., 2010; O'Connell et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2016; Werner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009; Noree et al., 2019; Noree et al., 2010; O'Connell et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2016; Werner et al., 2009).

claim: Filament assembly is typically induced by changes in metabolic conditions.
source: Filament assembly is typically induced by changes in metabolic conditions, and the enzymes involved are key regulatory or branch point enzymes, supporting the hypothesis that self-assembly is a general mechanism of regulating flux through specific metabolic pathways (Aughey and Liu, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Aughey and Liu, 2016).

claim: Metabolic filaments directly influence enzyme activity by stabilizing specific active or inhibited conformations.
source: In the few cases where the structure and function of metabolic filaments have been described, they show that the polymers directly influence enzyme activity by stabilizing specific active or inhibited conformations (Hunkeler et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Stoddard et al., 2019; Webb et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Hunkeler et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Stoddard et al., 2019; Webb et al., 2018).

claim: IMPDH2 filaments are flexible, adopting both active and inhibited conformations.
source: Low resolution structural studies have shown that IMPDH2 filaments are flexible, adopting both active and inhibited conformations, and that filament assembly does not directly affect enzyme activity (Anthony et al., 2017; Labesse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Anthony et al., 2017; Labesse et al., 2013).

claim: Filament assembly does not directly affect IMPDH2 enzyme activity.
source: Low resolution structural studies have shown that IMPDH2 filaments are flexible, adopting both active and inhibited conformations, and that filament assembly does not directly affect enzyme activity (Anthony et al., 2017; Labesse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Anthony et al., 2017; Labesse et al., 2013) and confirmed by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Guanine deprivation induces assembly of IMPDH into micron-scale ultrastructures composed of bundled filaments.
source: Guanine deprivation induces assembly of IMPDH into micron-scale ultrastructures composed of bundled filaments, which disassemble once homeostasis is restored (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Labesse et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Labesse et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2012).

claim: IMPDH filaments disassemble once homeostasis is restored.
source: Guanine deprivation induces assembly of IMPDH into micron-scale ultrastructures composed of bundled filaments, which disassemble once homeostasis is restored (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Labesse et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Labesse et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2012).

claim: Increased intracellular IMP results in IMPDH assembly.
source: Additional stimuli that alter IMPDH catalytic flux result in assembly, including increased intracellular IMP, and treatment with IMPDH inhibitors or other anti-proliferative drugs (Chang et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2006; Keppeke et al., 2015; Keppeke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Chang et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2006; Keppeke et al., 2015; Keppeke et al., 2018).

claim: Treatment with IMPDH inhibitors results in IMPDH assembly.
source: Additional stimuli that alter IMPDH catalytic flux result in assembly, including increased intracellular IMP, and treatment with IMPDH inhibitors or other anti-proliferative drugs (Chang et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2006; Keppeke et al., 2015; Keppeke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Chang et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2006; Keppeke et al., 2015; Keppeke et al., 2018).

claim: IMPDH assembly is correlated with proliferation of mouse induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: In vivo, IMPDH assembly is seen mainly in cases of high nucleotide demand, for example assembly is correlated with proliferation of mouse induced pluripotent stem cells and human T-cell activation (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Keppeke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Keppeke et al., 2018).

claim: IMPDH assembly is correlated with human T-cell activation.
source: In vivo, IMPDH assembly is seen mainly in cases of high nucleotide demand, for example assembly is correlated with proliferation of mouse induced pluripotent stem cells and human T-cell activation (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Keppeke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Keppeke et al., 2018).

claim: IMPDH forms stable tetramers.
source: IMPDH forms stable tetramers, each protomer consisting of a catalytic domain and a regulatory Bateman domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IMPDH structure and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Each IMPDH protomer consists of a catalytic domain and a regulatory Bateman domain.
source: IMPDH forms stable tetramers, each protomer consisting of a catalytic domain and a regulatory Bateman domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IMPDH structure and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: IMPDH converts IMP to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP).
source: The enzyme converts IMP to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) and requires NAD+ as a cofactor for a complex multi-stage catalysis requiring rearrangements of active site loops that close around the substrate upon binding, and then must reopen to allow release of product.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IMPDH catalytic mechanism.

claim: IMPDH requires NAD+ as a cofactor.
source: The enzyme converts IMP to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) and requires NAD+ as a cofactor for a complex multi-stage catalysis requiring rearrangements of active site loops that close around the substrate upon binding, and then must reopen to allow release of product.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IMPDH catalytic mechanism.

claim: The IMPDH regulatory domain contains three allosteric sites that bind adenine and guanine nucleotides.
source: The regulatory domain contains three allosteric sites that bind adenine and guanine nucleotides (Buey et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Buey et al., 2015b).

claim: Sites 1 and 2 are canonical cystathionine beta synthase motifs that bind either ATP/ADP or GTP/GDP.
source: Sites 1 and 2 are canonical cystathionine beta synthase motifs that bind either ATP/ADP or GTP/GDP, and are conserved among IMPDH homologues (Baykov et al., 2011; Ereño-Orbea et al., 2013; Ignoul and Eggermont, 2005; Scott et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Baykov et al., 2011; Ereño-Orbea et al., 2013; Ignoul and Eggermont, 2005; Scott et al., 2004).

claim: Sites 1 and 2 are conserved among IMPDH homologues.
source: Sites 1 and 2 are canonical cystathionine beta synthase motifs that bind either ATP/ADP or GTP/GDP, and are conserved among IMPDH homologues (Baykov et al., 2011; Ereño-Orbea et al., 2013; Ignoul and Eggermont, 2005; Scott et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Baykov et al., 2011; Ereño-Orbea et al., 2013; Ignoul and Eggermont, 2005; Scott et al., 2004).

claim: Site 3 is a non-canonical site located at the interface between domains that binds only GTP/GDP.
source: Site 3 is a non-canonical site located at the interface between domains that binds only GTP/GDP (Buey et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Buey et al., 2015b).

claim: In eukaryotes, adenine and guanine nucleotides allosterically modulate IMPDH activity by altering oligomeric state.
source: In eukaryotes, adenine and guanine nucleotides allosterically modulate IMPDH activity by altering oligomeric state (Buey et al., 2017; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Buey et al., 2017; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).

claim: IMPDH tetramers reversibly assemble into octamers when nucleotides bind the two canonical sites and drive dimerization of Bateman domains.
source: IMPDH tetramers reversibly assemble into octamers when nucleotides bind the two canonical sites and drive dimerization of Bateman domains (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Bound adenines promote an extended conformation in which the active sites are free to open and close as needed for catalysis.
source: Bound adenines promote an extended conformation in which the active sites are free to open and close as needed for catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: GTP/GDP binding induces a compressed conformation by changing the relative orientation of the two domains.
source: GTP/GDP binding induces a compressed conformation by changing the relative orientation of the two domains.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The compressed conformation brings the active sites of opposing tetramers tightly together, forming an interdigitated pseudo beta-barrel that prevents reopening and product release.
source: This brings the active sites of opposing tetramers tightly together, forming an interdigitated pseudo beta-barrel that prevents reopening and product release and inhibits IMPDH activity by a mechanism described as a 'conformational switch' between extended and compressed states (Buey et al., 2017; Buey et al., 2015b; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Buey et al., 2017; Buey et al., 2015b; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).

claim: The conformational switch between extended and compressed states inhibits IMPDH activity.
source: This brings the active sites of opposing tetramers tightly together, forming an interdigitated pseudo beta-barrel that prevents reopening and product release and inhibits IMPDH activity by a mechanism described as a 'conformational switch' between extended and compressed states (Buey et al., 2017; Buey et al., 2015b; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Buey et al., 2017; Buey et al., 2015b; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).

claim: The conformational switch is functionally relevant only in the octameric state.
source: Because inhibition requires interactions between two opposing tetramers, this switch is functionally relevant in only the octameric state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural mechanism described.

claim: In vitro treatment with ATP or GTP induces assembly of human IMPDH into filaments composed of stacked octamers interacting through their catalytic domains.
source: In vitro treatment with ATP or GTP induces assembly of human IMPDH into filaments composed of stacked octamers interacting through their catalytic domains (Figure 1D) (Anthony et al., 2017; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019; Labesse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Anthony et al., 2017; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019; Labesse et al., 2013) and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Filament segments can both extend and compress.
source: Filament segments can both extend and compress, and assembly does not have a direct effect on the activity of IMPDH2 (Anthony et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Anthony et al., 2017).

claim: Mutations that block assembly of IMPDH filaments in vitro also prevent assembly of the large IMPDH bundles observed in cells.
source: Importantly, mutations that block assembly of IMPDH filaments in vitro also prevent assembly of the large IMPDH bundles observed in cells, supporting the functional relevance of in vitro reconstituted filaments.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: In vitro IMPDH2 filament assembly is sensitive to high IMP levels.
source: These structures define the interactions that drive filament assembly, and we show that in vitro IMPDH2 filament assembly is sensitive to the same conditions that promote assembly in cells: high IMP levels and low guanine nucleotide levels (Keppeke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In vitro IMPDH2 filament assembly is sensitive to low guanine nucleotide levels.
source: These structures define the interactions that drive filament assembly, and we show that in vitro IMPDH2 filament assembly is sensitive to the same conditions that promote assembly in cells: high IMP levels and low guanine nucleotide levels (Keppeke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Filament assembly tunes sensitivity to GTP inhibition by stabilizing a conformation that reduces affinity for GTP.
source: Finally, we show that filament assembly tunes sensitivity to GTP inhibition by stabilizing a conformation that reduces affinity for GTP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: The resistance to feedback inhibition observed in IMPDH2 filaments demonstrates a new role for enzyme self-assembly.
source: In other enzyme polymers with known functions, assembly directly up or down regulates activity; the resistance to feedback inhibition observed in IMPDH2 filaments demonstrates a new role for enzyme self-assembly and reflects the diversity of allosteric regulatory mechanisms in metabolic filaments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing IMPDH2 to other metabolic filaments.

claim: ATP concentrations as low as 1 μM are sufficient to induce IMPDH2 filament assembly.
source: The affinity of IMPDH2 for ATP has not been directly measured but we found ATP concentrations as low as 1 μM sufficient to induce assembly (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IMPDH2 filaments are extremely flexible in the absence of other ligands.
source: We prepared cryo-EM grids of ATP-assembled filaments and found that in the absence of other ligands, IMPDH2 filaments are extremely flexible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IMPDH2 filaments are composed of conformationally heterogeneous octamers stacked head-to-head.
source: Two-dimensional class averages confirmed our prior observation from negative stain that the filaments are composed of conformationally heterogeneous octamers stacked head-to-head, resulting in flexible filaments with variable rise and radius of curvature (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is confirmed by 2D class averages shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Substrates did not have a direct effect on IMPDH2 filament assembly.
source: As previously reported, substrates did not have a direct effect on IMPDH2 filament assembly, and filament assembly did not directly affect enzymatic activity (Figure 2C–D) (Anthony et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C-D and supported by the citation (Anthony et al., 2017).

claim: Filament assembly did not directly affect IMPDH2 enzymatic activity.
source: As previously reported, substrates did not have a direct effect on IMPDH2 filament assembly, and filament assembly did not directly affect enzymatic activity (Figure 2C–D) (Anthony et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and supported by the citation (Anthony et al., 2017).

claim: The turnover rate observed for IMPDH2 is approximately 0.05 per second at room temperature.
source: While the turnover rate we observe here (~0.05 per second) is somewhat low, these reactions were performed near room temperature (24°C); we found that increasing reaction temperature to 37°C resulted in increasing Kcat to ~0.1 per second, roughly half what was observed in another recently published study of human IMPDH2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing reaction temperature to 37°C resulted in increasing Kcat to approximately 0.1 per second.
source: While the turnover rate we observe here (~0.05 per second) is somewhat low, these reactions were performed near room temperature (24°C); we found that increasing reaction temperature to 37°C resulted in increasing Kcat to ~0.1 per second, roughly half what was observed in another recently published study of human IMPDH2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of IMP and NAD+ did not significantly reduce filament flexibility.
source: Unfortunately, addition of IMP and NAD+, either alone or in combination, did not significantly reduce filament flexibility (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is an observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The filament assembly interface region was better resolved than other regions of the filaments.
source: From these 2D class averages we observed that filament flexibility was due to variations in the conformation of filament segments, but that the interface between segments did not vary, and as a consequence this region was better resolved (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from 2D class averages shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ATP/IMP/NAD+ consensus filament assembly interface was resolved at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: We determined the structure of the ATP/IMP/NAD+ consensus filament assembly interface at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: The filament assembly interface is composed of two symmetrically opposed catalytic domain tetramers.
source: This D4 symmetric region is composed of two symmetrically opposed catalytic domain tetramers.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The interface between tetramers is formed by the 12 amino-terminal residues of eight protomers.
source: The interface between tetramers is formed by the 12 amino-terminal residues of eight protomers, which each extend from the core of the molecule to bind one catalytic domain on the opposite tetramer, in a shallow surface groove formed by a short helix (476-485), two beta strands (51-63), and two short loops (355-360, 379-380) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A key tyrosine/arginine interaction (Y12/R356') anchors the filament assembly interface.
source: A key tyrosine/arginine interaction (Y12/R356') anchors the attachment; mutation of either of these residues to alanine was previously shown to abolish assembly, both in vivo and in vitro (Anthony et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by prior mutagenesis data cited (Anthony et al., 2017).

claim: Mutation of Y12 or R356 to alanine abolishes IMPDH2 filament assembly both in vivo and in vitro.
source: A key tyrosine/arginine interaction (Y12/R356') anchors the attachment; mutation of either of these residues to alanine was previously shown to abolish assembly, both in vivo and in vitro (Anthony et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Anthony et al., 2017).

claim: The overall surface area buried by a single filament assembly interaction is 2,300 Å2.
source: The overall surface area buried by a single interaction is 2,300 Å2, with a total buried area of 9,200 Å2 for the multimeric interface.
evidence: This is a calculation from the structural data.

claim: The total buried area for the multimeric filament assembly interface is 9,200 Å2.
source: The overall surface area buried by a single interaction is 2,300 Å2, with a total buried area of 9,200 Å2 for the multimeric interface.
evidence: This is a calculation from the structural data.

claim: The N-terminal tail of IMPDH is the least conserved part of the protein.
source: The N-terminal tail of IMPDH, corresponding to residues 1–28 in IMPDH2, is the least conserved part of the protein, with large variation in length and sequence between phyla, as well as conformational variation among known structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) (Buey et al., 2015a; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2017; Labesse et al., 2013; Makowska-Grzyska et al., 2015; Osipiuk et al., 2014; Prosise and Luecke, 2003; Trapero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The residues involved in filament contacts are conserved among chordates.
source: The residues involved in filament contacts, however, are conserved among chordates, consistent with the fact that IMPDH polymerization has only been reported in vertebrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: IMPDH polymerization has only been reported in vertebrates.
source: The residues involved in filament contacts, however, are conserved among chordates, consistent with the fact that IMPDH polymerization has only been reported in vertebrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: In the filament structure, the N-terminal tail is rotated about 30° compared to crystal structures.
source: In the filament structure, however, the Val13/Pro14 contacts are broken and the entire tail is rotated about 30° to position Tyr12 to contact Arg356 across the filament interface (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The catalytic domain in the consensus structure is nearly identical to a structure of human IMPDH2 bound to competitive inhibitors (PDB 1nf7, backbone RMSD 0.641 Å).
source: In this consensus structure, the remainder of the catalytic domain is nearly identical to a structure of human hIMPDH2 bound to competitive inhibitors in a previously determined crystal structure (PDB 1nf7, backbone RMSD 0.641 Å for residues 18–107, 245–417, and 439–514) (Sintchak et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a structural comparison to a published structure (Sintchak et al., 1996).

claim: There is strong density in both the IMP and NAD+ binding sites.
source: There is strong density in the both the IMP and NAD+ binding sites.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density.

claim: The enzyme filaments were actively turning over when flash frozen.
source: We have modeled these ligands as IMP and NAD+, however because the enzyme filaments were actively turning over when flash frozen, we have likely captured a mixture of substrate-, intermediate-, and product-bound states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental conditions.

claim: A fully extended D4-symmetric octamer was resolved at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: The most well-resolved was a D4-symmetric, fully extended octamer (3.3 Å, Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: The eight Bateman domains are symmetrically extended with respect to their catalytic domains, giving the octameric segment a helical rise of 118 Å.
source: The eight Bateman domains are symmetrically extended with respect to their catalytic domains, giving the octameric segment a helical rise of 118 Å; a symmetric helix of these segments would have a twist of 36°.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: There is strong density at both canonical ATP-binding sites within the Bateman domain.
source: There is strong density at both of the canonical ATP-binding sites within the Bateman domain (Figure 3F), consistent with previous crystal structures of ATP/ADP-bound fungal and bacterial IMPDH (Buey et al., 2017; Labesse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 3F, consistent with prior structures.

claim: A bent filament segment structure was resolved at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: We also resolved several bent filament segment structures, the best resolved of which reached 3.9 Å (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3G and supplementary figures.

claim: The bent octamer contains two identical tetramers, with three protomers in extended conformations and one in the compressed conformation.
source: This bent octamer contains two identical tetramers. For each, three protomers are in extended conformations, while one protomer is in the compressed conformation.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: These are the first structures of IMPDH in the compressed conformation in the absence of guanine nucleotides.
source: To our knowledge, these are the first structure of IMPDH in the compressed conformation in the absence of guanine nucleotides.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the structures based on comparison to prior literature.

claim: The third Bateman binding site remains unoccupied in the compressed conformation in the absence of GTP.
source: While the two canonical ATP sites are occupied, the third Bateman binding site (which forms only in the compressed state and is GTP/GDP-specific) remains unoccupied.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Protomers within ATP-bound IMPDH filaments readily sample the compressed conformation.
source: This suggests that protomers within ATP-bound IMPDH filaments readily sample the compressed conformation, and that GTP binding to site 3 selectively stabilizes this state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: GTP binding to site 3 selectively stabilizes the compressed state.
source: This suggests that protomers within ATP-bound IMPDH filaments readily sample the compressed conformation, and that GTP binding to site 3 selectively stabilizes this state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: A compressed protomer can form a Bateman dimer with an extended partner.
source: Further, the ability of a compressed protomer to form a Bateman dimer with an extended partner demonstrates a lack of conformational cooperativity across the Bateman domain interface.
evidence: This is a structural observation that leads to an inference about cooperativity.

claim: There is a lack of conformational cooperativity across the Bateman domain interface.
source: Further, the ability of a compressed protomer to form a Bateman dimer with an extended partner demonstrates a lack of conformational cooperativity across the Bateman domain interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: As little as 10 μM IMP inhibits filament disassembly by GTP.
source: In the absence of substrate, GTP induces disassembly of filaments, but as little as 10 μM IMP inhibits disassembly (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Pre-treatment of filaments with IMP prevents disassembly by GTP.
source: Pre-treatment of filaments with IMP prevents disassembly by GTP, and addition of IMP promotes reassembly of filaments previously disassembled by GTP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Addition of IMP promotes reassembly of filaments previously disassembled by GTP.
source: Pre-treatment of filaments with IMP prevents disassembly by GTP, and addition of IMP promotes reassembly of filaments previously disassembled by GTP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The ATP/GTP/IMP filament assembly interface map (3.0 Å) is identical to the ATP/IMP/NAD+ filament interface (backbone RMSD = 0.407).
source: The ATP/GTP/IMP filament assembly interface map (3.0 Å) is identical (backbone RMSD = 0.407) to the ATP/IMP/NAD+ filament interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a structural comparison from cryo-EM data.

claim: A 3.2 Å structure of a fully compressed filament segment was obtained.
source: Classifying the most well-resolved filament segments as before, we obtained a 3.2 Å structure of a fully compressed filament segment (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: The Bateman domains are symmetrically compressed, with ligand density at all three allosteric sites.
source: The Bateman domains are symmetrically compressed, with ligand density at all three allosteric sites.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The active site is well resolved, including the canonical interactions between opposing active site fingers that inhibit catalysis.
source: The active site is well resolved, including the canonical interactions between opposing active site fingers that inhibit catalysis by preventing catalytic dynamics (Buey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure, consistent with prior work (Buey et al., 2017).

claim: GTP-saturated, +IMP filaments were shorter in length compared to uninhibited filament datasets.
source: Compared to the uninhibited filament datasets, these GTP-saturated, +IMP filaments were shorter in length.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: A 3.3 Å structure of filament ends was resolved.
source: The best-resolved structure of these filament ends (3.3 Å) is conformationally similar to the filament segments, being fully compressed, with well-resolved IMP-bound active sites in the inhibited conformation; however, without the filament assembly interface, the N-terminus is only partially resolved (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4D and supplementary figures.

claim: The best resolved free octamer class reached intermediate resolution (4.5 Å).
source: The best resolved free octamer class reached intermediate resolution (4.5 Å) (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4E and supplementary figures.

claim: The free octamer is conformationally similar to a crystal structure of IMPDH2 bound to GTP (PDB 6i0o, backbone RMSD = 0.978 Å).
source: This octamer is conformationally similar (backbone RMSD = 0.978 Å) to a recent higher-resolution crystal structure of IMPDH2 bound to GTP (PDB 6i0o) (Buey et al., 2017; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a structural comparison to published structures.

claim: Without IMP present, the active site loops of the free octamers are disordered.
source: Without IMP present, the active site loops of the free octamers are disordered, with partial density for the fingers extending across to the opposing tetramer.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The filament interface of the inhibited segments is unchanged from the uninhibited filaments.
source: The filament interface of the inhibited segments is unchanged from the uninhibited filaments (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 4F.

claim: At the free filament ends the N-terminus is only partially resolved (a.a. 1–11).
source: However, at the free filament ends the N-terminus is only partially unresolved (a.a. 1–11), with the resolvable portion rotated ~30° degrees compared to the bound interface, such that Val13 inserts into the shallow hydrophobic pocket formed by A307, A308, and Lys311 of the neighboring protomer, very similar to its position in the GTP-bound free octamer crystal structure (PDB 6i0o) (Figure 4G) (Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 4G, compared to a published structure.

claim: Each protomer of the free octamer and at filament ends is tilted ~5° relative to the four-fold symmetry axis.
source: Each protomer of the free octamer and at filament ends is tilted ~5° relative to the four-fold symmetry axis, such that the tetramer becomes more 'bowed' than the 'flat' tetramers at filament assembly interfaces (Figure 4I, Video 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 4I and Video 1.

claim: The bowed tetramer conformation and the filament assembly interface are mutually exclusive.
source: The bowed tetramer conformation and the filament assembly interface are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: The flat conformation promotes release of the N-termini from their binding sites on neighboring protomers.
source: Thus the flat conformation promotes release of the N-termini from their binding sites on neighboring protomers, freeing them to rotate into the conformation seen in the assembled filament interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Bowed tetramers cannot form the IMPDH2 filament assembly interface.
source: Thus bowed tetramers cannot form the IMPDH2 filament assembly interface, and tetramer flattening is a necessary precondition for IMPDH2 filament assembly (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Tetramer flattening is a necessary precondition for IMPDH2 filament assembly.
source: Thus bowed tetramers cannot form the IMPDH2 filament assembly interface, and tetramer flattening is a necessary precondition for IMPDH2 filament assembly (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations shown in Figure 4J.

claim: In the absence of substrate, GTP induces both compression of filament segments and tetramer bowing.
source: In the absence of substrate, GTP induces both compression of filament segments and tetramer bowing, with the latter resulting in filament disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data and experimental observations.

claim: When IMP is bound, the disordered active site loops become ordered and rigid.
source: But when IMP is bound, the disordered active site loops become ordered and rigid, buttressing intra-tetramer contacts as well as forming a pseudo-beta-barrel between opposing tetramers in the GTP-bound state.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: IMP binding increases contacts that work to resist tetramer bowing.
source: These increased contacts work to resist tetramer bowing and more readily sample the flat tetramer conformation, which promotes, and is stabilized by, the filament assembly interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: When IMP levels are low, GTP promotes filament disassembly.
source: When IMP levels are low, GTP promotes filament disassembly, but high IMP levels shift the equilibrium towards filament assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: High IMP levels shift the equilibrium towards filament assembly.
source: When IMP levels are low, GTP promotes filament disassembly, but high IMP levels shift the equilibrium towards filament assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Wild-type IMPDH2 enzyme is less sensitive to GTP inhibition compared with Y12A.
source: To probe whether filament assembly influences the regulatory effects of GTP on IMPDH2 activity we compared enzyme kinetics of the wildtype enzyme with the non-assembling mutant Y12A. We measured the GTP dose-response of IMPDH2 pre-incubated with varying levels of ATP, and found that wild-type enzyme is less sensitive to GTP inhibition, compared with Y12A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The apparent GTP IC50 of wild-type IMPDH2 is roughly two-fold lower than for Y12A, depending on ATP concentration.
source: Depending on ATP concentration, the apparent GTP IC50 of the wild-type was roughly two-fold lower than for Y12A.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the kinetic assays.

claim: At higher ATP levels, the apparent GTP IC50 of WT and the non-assembly mutant both increase.
source: At higher ATP levels, the apparent GTP IC50 of WT and the non-assembly mutant both increase.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the kinetic assays.

claim: GTP inhibition of IMPDH2 is affected by ATP independent of filament assembly.
source: We attribute this to competition between ATP and GTP at the first and second Bateman sites, suggesting that independent of filament assembly, GTP inhibition of IMPDH2 is affected by ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: The range of GTP in which substrate-saturated filaments resist GTP inhibition is within the upper range of in vivo concentrations.
source: Notably, the range of GTP in which the substrate-saturated filaments resist GTP inhibition is within the upper range of in vivo concentrations (Traut, 1994).
evidence: This is a comparison to published in vivo data (Traut, 1994).

claim: One function of IMPDH2 filaments is to resist inhibition by GTP.
source: One function, then, of IMPDH2 filaments is to resist inhibition by GTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic and structural data.

claim: Uninhibited filaments were often extended.
source: As in the cryo-EM datasets, we found that uninhibited filaments were often extended, and fully inhibited filaments were universally compressed.
evidence: This is an observation from negative stain EM shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fully inhibited filaments were universally compressed.
source: As in the cryo-EM datasets, we found that uninhibited filaments were often extended, and fully inhibited filaments were universally compressed.
evidence: This is an observation from negative stain EM shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Partially inhibited filaments contained a more heterogeneous mix of extended, bent, and compressed segments.
source: However, we noted that the partially inhibited filaments contained a more heterogeneous mix of extended, bent, and compressed segments.
evidence: This is an observation from negative stain EM shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Depending on the degree of extension/bending/compression, filament segments exhibit a range of increasingly stronger interactions between opposing catalytic domains.
source: Depending on the degree of extension/bending/compression, filament segments exhibit a range of increasingly stronger interactions between opposing catalytic domains.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 5E.

claim: For fully extended segments, there are no interactions between opposing catalytic domains, and the flexible active loops are able to perform the complex conformational changes necessary for catalysis.
source: For the fully extended segments, there are no interactions, and the flexible active loops are able to perform the complex conformational changes necessary for catalysis (Buey et al., 2017; Hedstrom, 2009).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by prior knowledge (Buey et al., 2017; Hedstrom, 2009).

claim: For active sites that make contacts in compressed states, activity is likely impaired because the active site loops are constrained.
source: For the active sites that make these contacts, activity is likely impaired because the active site loops are constrained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The presence of some unconstrained active sites in bent filament segments means that these protomers are catalytically active.
source: However, the presence of some unconstrained active sites in the bent filament segments means that these protomers are catalytically active.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The effect of compression on activity is not cooperative within the octamers.
source: This effect is not cooperative within the octamers, and even a single extended protomer is sufficient to reduce inhibitory active site contacts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Filament assembly promotes the extended state of individual protomers, which reduces overall GTP affinity due to disruption of site 3.
source: Thus filament assembly promotes the extended state of individual protomers, which reduces overall GTP affinity due to disruption of site 3.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observations shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Conformational changes are not cooperative across the filament interface.
source: The results of the classification against synthetic templates are in line with the experimentally derived classifications for each dataset, but we did not find a strong correlation in segment conformation along filaments, suggesting that conformational changes are not cooperative across the filament interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the classification analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 8-13.

claim: IMPDH activity is upregulated to increase guanine levels in proliferating tissues like tumors and regenerating liver.
source: IMPDH activity is upregulated to increase guanine levels in proliferating tissues like tumors and regenerating liver (He et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018; Nagai et al., 1991; Tressler et al., 1994; Yalowitz and Jayaram, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (He et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018; Nagai et al., 1991; Tressler et al., 1994; Yalowitz and Jayaram, 2000).

claim: T-cell activation is dependent on increased production of purine nucleotides.
source: IMPDH plays a particularly important role in the immune response, where T-cell activation is dependant on increased production of purine nucleotides, and is associated with IMPDH filament assembly (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2000; Zimmermann et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2000; Zimmermann et al., 1998).

claim: T-cell activation is associated with IMPDH filament assembly.
source: IMPDH plays a particularly important role in the immune response, where T-cell activation is dependant on increased production of purine nucleotides, and is associated with IMPDH filament assembly (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2000; Zimmermann et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2000; Zimmermann et al., 1998).

claim: IMPDH is the target of several drugs used in immunosuppressive treatment of autoimmune disease and organ transplant rejection.
source: As a result, IMPDH is the target of several drugs used in immunosuppressive treatment of both autoimmune disease and organ transplant rejection, and is considered a promising target for antineoplastic agents (Bergan et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2017; Shu and Nair, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Bergan et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2017; Shu and Nair, 2008).

claim: IMPDH is considered a promising target for antineoplastic agents.
source: As a result, IMPDH is the target of several drugs used in immunosuppressive treatment of both autoimmune disease and organ transplant rejection, and is considered a promising target for antineoplastic agents (Bergan et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2017; Shu and Nair, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Bergan et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2017; Shu and Nair, 2008).

claim: Assembly and disassembly of IMPDH into filaments has been observed in healthy proliferative cells and in cancer cells.
source: Assembly and disassembly of IMPDH into filaments has been observed in healthy proliferative cells, and in cancer cells (Keppeke et al., 2018; Wolfe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Keppeke et al., 2018; Wolfe et al., 2019).

claim: IMPDH filaments reversibly assemble in stimulated T-cells as they transition to a proliferative state.
source: IMPDH filaments reversibly assemble in stimulated T-cells as they transition to a proliferative state, in a mechanism dependent on multiple metabolic signaling pathways and on the levels of guanine nucleotides (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Calise et al., 2018; Duong-Ly et al., 2018).

claim: IMPDH2 filament assembly reduces feedback inhibition of enzyme activity in a substrate-dependent manner.
source: We propose a model that describes the regulatory role of human IMPDH2 filament assembly, in which assembly reduces feedback inhibition of enzyme activity in a substrate-dependant manner, increasing flux through the de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis pathway in response to proliferative signaling.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the structural and biochemical data.

claim: IMPDH2 filament assembly increases flux through the de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis pathway in response to proliferative signaling.
source: We propose a model that describes the regulatory role of human IMPDH2 filament assembly, in which assembly reduces feedback inhibition of enzyme activity in a substrate-dependant manner, increasing flux through the de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis pathway in response to proliferative signaling.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the structural and biochemical data.

claim: In the absence of either IMP or guanine ligands, IMPDH2 is conformationally dynamic.
source: In the absence of either IMP or guanine ligands, IMPDH2 is conformationally dynamic (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Apo IMPDH2 forms stable tetramers, which freely sample both the 'bowed' and 'flat' tetramer conformations.
source: Apo IMPDH2 forms stable tetramers, which freely sample both the 'bowed' and 'flat' tetramer conformations, with the latter resulting in release of the N-terminus and assembly into stable interfacial octamers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claim: Adenine nucleotides bind with high affinity to the Bateman domain, resulting in stable filaments in which the active site loops remain unconstrained and the enzyme is active.
source: Adenine nucleotides bind with high affinity to the Bateman domain, resulting in stable filaments in which the active site loops remain unconstrained and the enzyme is active.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The ATP concentration required to induce filament assembly in vitro is far below the expected in vivo levels.
source: The ATP concentration required to induce filament assembly in vitro is far below the expected in vivo levels; we thus predict the apo state to be rare in human cells (Traut, 1994).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison to published in vivo concentrations (Traut, 1994).

claim: Without bound guanine nucleotides, the Bateman domains of individual protomers freely compress and extend.
source: Without bound guanine nucleotides, the Bateman domains of individual protomers freely compress and extend (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The flat tetramer conformation found in assembled IMPDH2 filaments is resistant to full compression of octameric filament segments.
source: However, the flat tetramer conformation found in assembled IMPDH2 filaments is resistant to full compression of octameric filament segments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claim: Binding of GTP to the Bateman domain stabilizes the compressed state, leading to lattice strain that is relieved by disassembly of the filament interface and tetramer bowing.
source: Binding of GTP to the Bateman domain stabilizes the compressed state, leading to lattice strain that is relieved by disassembly of the filament interface and tetramer bowing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claim: High intracellular guanine levels disassemble IMPDH2 filaments into stable free octamers whose activity is inhibited.
source: In this way high intracellular guanine levels disassemble IMPDH2 filaments into stable free octamers whose activity is inhibited.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Binding of IMP to the active site stabilizes the flexible active site loops.
source: Binding of IMP to the active site stabilizes the flexible active site loops, and saturation with both IMP and GTP results in compressed filaments in which the active sites of opposing tetramers interlock into a stable network.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Saturation with both IMP and GTP results in compressed filaments in which the active sites of opposing tetramers interlock into a stable network.
source: Binding of IMP to the active site stabilizes the flexible active site loops, and saturation with both IMP and GTP results in compressed filaments in which the active sites of opposing tetramers interlock into a stable network.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: IMP-saturated compressed filaments resist the lattice strain brought on by compression, blocking GTP-induced filament disassembly.
source: This rigidifies the octameric filament segment, which now resists the lattice strain brought on by compression, blocking GTP-induced filament disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, the salvage pathways provide sufficient purine nucleotides, and IMP production is low.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, the salvage pathways provide sufficient purine nucleotides, and IMP production is low.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleotide metabolism.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions IMPDH2 is bound to both adenine and guanine nucleotides, but not IMP, forming free octamers rather than filaments.
source: Under these conditions IMPDH2 is bound to both adenine and guanine nucleotides, but not IMP, forming free octamers rather than filaments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model developed from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: In vivo, filaments are typically not observed in quiescent cells.
source: In vivo, filaments are typically not observed in quiescent cells; rather, as in our model, their assembly is associated with increased intracellular IMP and decreased intracellular GTP (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Keppeke et al., 2018; Schiavon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Keppeke et al., 2018; Schiavon et al., 2018).

claim: IMPDH filament assembly is associated with increased intracellular IMP and decreased intracellular GTP.
source: In vivo, filaments are typically not observed in quiescent cells; rather, as in our model, their assembly is associated with increased intracellular IMP and decreased intracellular GTP (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Keppeke et al., 2018; Schiavon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Calise et al., 2014; Juda et al., 2014; Keppeke et al., 2018; Schiavon et al., 2018).

claim: Depletion of guanine allows Bateman domain extension, and transient assembly into enzymatically active filaments.
source: Depletion of guanine allows Bateman domain extension, and transient assembly into enzymatically active filaments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model developed from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Upon restoration of guanine levels, active filaments disassemble into compressed free octamers.
source: However, upon restoration of guanine levels, these active filaments disassemble into compressed free octamers, mirroring the known feedback inhibition behavior of non-filament forming IMPDH homologues (Buey et al., 2017; Buey et al., 2015b; Fernández-Justel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model and comparison to other IMPDH homologues.

claim: IMP-saturated IMPDH2 filaments resist both disassembly and the fully compressed, inhibited state.
source: IMP-saturated IMPDH2 filaments resist both disassembly and the fully compressed, inhibited state.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: Even at elevated guanine nucleotide levels, IMP-saturated filaments retain a proportion of uninhibited active sites.
source: Even at elevated guanine nucleotide levels, these filaments retain a proportion of uninhibited active sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claim: IMPDH2 filament assembly serves to elevate intracellular guanine nucleotide levels during the proliferative state by resisting feedback inhibition.
source: Our data strongly support the idea that IMPDH2 filament assembly serves to elevate intracellular guanine nucleotide levels during the proliferative state by resisting feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the data.

claim: Production of IMP is upregulated in response to overall purine demand, as well as in response to proliferative signaling via mTOR.
source: Production of IMP is upregulated in response to overall purine demand, as well as in response to proliferative signaling via the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) (Ben-Sahra et al., 2016; Smith, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Ben-Sahra et al., 2016; Smith, 1998).

claim: Inhibition of mTOR reverses IMPDH filament assembly in activated mouse T-cells and proliferating mouse liver cells.
source: Inhibition of mTOR reverses IMPDH filament assembly in activated mouse T-cells, as well as proliferating mouse liver cells (Chang et al., 2015; Duong-Ly et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (Chang et al., 2015; Duong-Ly et al., 2018).

claim: The dependence of filament assembly on IMP levels provides an avenue for regulation of assembly through established proliferative signaling pathways.
source: Thus the dependence of filament assembly on IMP levels provides an avenue for regulation of assembly through established proliferative signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings and comparison to known signaling pathways.

claim: IMPDH2 filaments fine-tune the allosteric response by reducing affinity for inhibitory downstream products.
source: Instead, as we have shown here, IMPDH2 filaments fine-tune the the allosteric response by reducing affinity for inhibitory downstream products.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the data.

claim: IMPDH2 filament assembly represents a new way in which enzyme self-assembly can modulate flux through metabolic pathways.
source: This represents a new way in which enzyme self-assembly can modulate flux through metabolic pathways, providing an additional layer of regulatory control on top of existing transcriptional, post-translational, and allosteric regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of the findings.
